lessons.title: Describe a chart with an overview and accurate comparisons
lessons.purpose: Select the main pattern in a simple dataset and explain changes without inventing causes.
explanation: Begin by identifying what is measured, the units, the groups and the time period. An overview describes the most important pattern across the data. Supporting paragraphs then give selected values and comparisons. An overview is not a list of every number, and a data description is not an explanation of causes unless the supplied information supports them.

Percentage points and percentage change answer different questions. A rise from 40% to 55% is an increase of 15 percentage points. Relative to the starting share, the increase is 15 divided by 40, or 37.5%. State which measure you mean. Use approximate language only when appropriate to the precision shown.

For IELTS Academic Writing Task 1, current official guidance requires at least 150 words. The complete model below is an original example using invented data; it has not been scored by an IELTS examiner. The principle also applies to university reports, where the assignment may have different length and formatting requirements.

language_pattern.form: Introduction to data → overview → selected comparisons with units.
language_pattern.meaning: Lead with the pattern, then show the evidence.
language_pattern.limits: The dataset describes reported travel mode, not causes, journey frequency or environmental effects.

worked_examples.title: A complete original data description
worked_examples.context: Invented campus survey: main travel mode (%). 2015: bus 40, walking 20, car 40. 2020: bus 50, walking 25, car 25. 2025: bus 55, walking 30, car 15. Each annual sample contains 1,000 respondents and each row totals 100%.
worked_examples.model:
The table compares the percentages of respondents who reported travelling mainly by bus, on foot or by car in three campus surveys conducted in 2015, 2020 and 2025. Each survey included 1,000 respondents.

Overall, bus use and walking became more common, while the proportion travelling mainly by car fell. Bus travel was the largest category in the final two surveys, and by 2025 it accounted for more than half of the responses.

In 2015, buses and cars each represented 40% of the sample, whereas walking accounted for the remaining 20%. Five years later, the bus share had risen to 50%. Walking and car travel were then equal at 25% each.

By 2025, the proportion reporting bus travel had reached 55%, and walking had increased to 30%. Car travel, in contrast, had declined to 15%, a fall of 25 percentage points from its initial level. Across the full period, the increase in walking was steady, at five percentage points between each pair of surveys, while the growth in bus use slowed in the second interval.
annotations: The introduction identifies the measure and dates.
The overview names the main directions without inventing reasons.
The detail paragraphs select useful comparisons and retain percentage units.
The ending compares changes across intervals; it does not add an unsupported opinion.
worked_examples.meaning: A complete description can be organised and selective while remaining faithful to every stated number.

worked_examples.title: Distinguish two ways to describe a change
worked_examples.context: The bus share rises from 40% to 55%.
worked_examples.model: The bus share increased by 15 percentage points, equivalent to a 37.5% increase relative to its original share.
annotations: 55 minus 40 gives 15 percentage points.
15 divided by 40, multiplied by 100, gives the relative percentage change.
Neither value is a claim that the number of bus journeys rose by that amount.
worked_examples.meaning: Name the denominator and the quantity being compared.

common_mistakes.revision: The bus share increased by 15 percentage points.
common_mistakes.reason: The first wording confuses a difference between percentages with a relative change.

common_mistakes.draft: The survey proves that cheaper tickets caused the increase.
common_mistakes.revision: The survey shows an increase in the reported bus share.
common_mistakes.reason: Ticket prices and causation are not given in the dataset.

takeaways: Identify the unit before describing change.
Give an overview before selected details.
Do not invent a cause to make a description sound complete.

lessons.title: Explain a process and report completed work
lessons.purpose: Describe a sequence accurately, with clear units and a deliberate choice of time and voice.
explanation: A process description explains how stages relate. Start with the input and destination, then follow a meaningful order. Use sequence expressions where they help, but avoid beginning every sentence with then. A reference such as the combined stream can connect stages naturally.

A general description often uses the present tense; a record of completed work commonly uses the past. Active and passive forms can both be appropriate. “The mixer combines the streams” and “The streams are combined” differ in focus. Neither is automatically more accurate. Preserve the actual method, measurements and conditions when writing a real report.

Numbers need units and a clear basis. In a mass-fraction example, 20% by mass means 20 units of solute mass in 100 units of total solution mass. A language model should not conceal an arithmetic inconsistency. The worked calculation below is an invented idealised mixer with no accumulation, reaction or material loss; it is not a laboratory operating procedure.

language_pattern.form: Identify the input → describe the sequence → give the output → state relevant assumptions.
language_pattern.meaning: Help the reader follow both language and physical meaning.
language_pattern.limits: Use only the real method and conditions in an actual report. Never invent a completed procedure.

worked_examples.title: Explain an idealised mixer
worked_examples.context: Invented data: feed A is 100 kg/h and contains 20% solute by mass; feed B is 50 kg/h of pure water. There is one outlet and no accumulation or loss.
worked_examples.model: Two streams enter an idealised mixer. Feed A flows at 100 kg/h and contains 20% solute by mass, while feed B supplies 50 kg/h of pure water. The streams combine to produce an outlet flow of 150 kg/h. The solute flow remains 20 kg/h, giving an outlet mass fraction of 20/150, or approximately 13.3%. This calculation assumes no accumulation, reaction or material loss.
annotations: The inputs are named before the output.
While contrasts the two feed compositions without suggesting a time conflict.
100 × 0.20 gives 20 kg/h of solute; 100 + 50 gives 150 kg/h total.
Approximately signals rounding of 13.333…%.
worked_examples.meaning: The paragraph communicates a model and its assumptions, not a claim that an experiment was performed.

worked_examples.title: Describe completed work with the correct focus
worked_examples.context: Invented completed classroom activity: a student team compared two supplied graphs and documented their labels.
worked_examples.model: The team compared the two supplied graphs and recorded the axis labels in a table. Each value was checked against its stated unit before the comparison was written.
annotations: Past tense identifies completed work in this fictional example.
The first sentence names who acted.
The passive in the second sentence keeps attention on the values.
worked_examples.meaning: A report can combine voices while maintaining a consistent time frame.

common_mistakes.revision: The outlet mass flow is 150 kg/h.
common_mistakes.reason: The quantity and unit make the number meaningful.

common_mistakes.draft: A past-tense method is wrong because scientific writing must be present passive.
common_mistakes.revision: Use the tense and voice that fit the actual purpose and reporting convention.
common_mistakes.reason: Completed work and a general process are different communicative situations.

takeaways: Follow the process in a logical order.
State quantities with units and a basis.
Keep assumptions and observed facts distinct.

lessons.title: Develop a position in a complete essay
lessons.purpose: State a qualified position, develop reasons and respond to a relevant limitation.
explanation: An opinion essay needs a position that answers the assigned issue. Develop a small number of relevant reasons with explanation and examples. A list of claims is not a developed argument. A useful example makes the reasoning visible; it does not need an invented statistic or a fictitious research citation.

A qualified position can be clear: support an action under stated conditions, or support part of a proposal while rejecting another part. A counterargument matters when it could change the judgement. Explain its significance and your response rather than adding “some people disagree” as a decorative sentence.

Current IELTS Academic Writing Task 2 guidance requires at least 250 words. The original model below exceeds that minimum, but word count does not establish quality or predict a band. Its paragraph structure is one workable choice, not a universal template to memorise. Real coursework must meet its own evidence and citation requirements.

language_pattern.form: Position → developed reason → further reason or limitation → reasoned conclusion.
language_pattern.meaning: Make the judgement and its support easy to follow.
language_pattern.limits: Do not invent research evidence or imply that the model has an examiner-awarded score.

worked_examples.title: A complete original opinion essay
worked_examples.context: Issue for the model: a university is considering making recordings of lecture introductions available alongside ordinary classes.
worked_examples.model:
Universities should make recordings of lecture introductions available when they can do so responsibly. These recordings should support normal classes rather than replace opportunities to ask questions and discuss difficult ideas. Their value lies in improving access to the starting point of a lesson, while their limitations require careful attention.

One benefit is that students can return to unfamiliar terminology. A learner who understands an argument but misses one definition may struggle with everything that follows. A short recording allows that learner to revisit the definition before reading the course material. For example, a student encountering a new statistical term could listen again and then connect it to the worked example discussed in class. This is a practical use of repetition, not a reason to assume that watching alone produces understanding.

Recordings can also help students prepare for discussion. If an introduction explains the purpose and basic vocabulary of a topic, classroom time can be used to examine examples and address uncertainty. However, this arrangement works only when students can access the recording and the introduction is clear enough to use independently. Captions and a readable summary can help students who cannot easily use audio in their current setting.

There are also limits. A recording cannot respond to an unexpected misunderstanding, and a student may feel familiar with the language without being able to use the idea. Teachers therefore still need opportunities to explain, discuss and respond. The university should also make clear which material is available and how students are expected to use it.

In conclusion, recorded introductions can be a useful addition to university teaching when they are accessible and connected to the rest of the course. They should provide a reliable beginning for learning, while the wider teaching process continues to support explanation and discussion.
annotations: The opening states support with conditions.
The second paragraph develops one reason through a concrete example.
The third discusses preparation and access.
The fourth considers an important limitation.
The conclusion preserves the original qualified position.
worked_examples.meaning: The argument is supported by explained reasoning and hypothetical examples, not fabricated research results.

worked_examples.title: Make a position precise
worked_examples.context: Draft position: “Recordings are good and bad and people have different opinions.”
worked_examples.model: Recorded introductions are useful as an accessible supplement, but they should not replace opportunities for discussion.
annotations: Useful identifies the judgement.
As an accessible supplement states the condition.
The final clause makes the limit explicit.
worked_examples.meaning: A qualified position can be more precise than an absolute yes or no.

common_mistakes.draft: A longer essay always earns a higher score.
common_mistakes.revision: Develop a relevant, accurate response that meets the task requirements.
common_mistakes.reason: Length beyond the minimum is not proof of quality.

common_mistakes.revision: A student may benefit by revisiting unfamiliar terminology.
common_mistakes.reason: Do not invent a statistic or a source to strengthen the argument.

takeaways: State a position that answers the issue.
Explain how each example supports the reason.

lessons.title: Use evidence without overstating it
lessons.purpose: Compare sources according to what each can establish and state the limits of a conclusion.
explanation: A claim needs evidence relevant to that claim. Preferences can support a statement about what respondents like; they cannot by themselves establish an effect on performance. A measured association can be useful, but alternative explanations may remain. Name the population, conditions and outcome before deciding how strong a conclusion should be.

When several sources discuss a topic, organise the writing around the issue rather than giving one unrelated paragraph per source. Explain where the sources agree, what each contributes and why their limits matter. Disagreement can arise because they measured different outcomes or used different participants.

The two records below are fictional teaching data. In a real assignment, use traceable sources, inspect the relevant sections and follow the required citation style. A plausible title, quotation or publication date must never be invented to make a paragraph appear researched.

language_pattern.form: Claim + relevant evidence + explanation of the link + limitation.
language_pattern.meaning: Show why the evidence bears on the claim.
language_pattern.limits: Combining weak evidence does not automatically produce a strong conclusion.

worked_examples.title: Combine two kinds of information
worked_examples.context: Fictional training record A: 12 of 18 volunteers preferred a quiet study room. Record B: observers counted 24 occupied seats in that room and 20 in a discussion area on one Tuesday at 14:00.
worked_examples.model: The training records suggest interest in the quiet room, but they describe different outcomes. Record A reports a preference among a small volunteer group. Record B records occupancy at one time. Together they can inform a decision to investigate demand further; they do not demonstrate that the room improves grades or that demand is always higher.
annotations: The paragraph distinguishes preference from occupancy.
The sample and time limits are preserved.
The proposed next decision is proportionate to the evidence.
worked_examples.meaning: A useful synthesis can explain what remains unknown.

worked_examples.title: Avoid a causal leap
worked_examples.context: An invented observation finds that students who attend a study group also tend to submit more assignments.
worked_examples.model: Study-group attendance was associated with more frequent assignment submission in this observation. The result does not establish whether attendance caused the difference, because other factors may have influenced both.
annotations: Associated reports a relationship without asserting cause.
The outcome is assignment submission, not grades.
The limitation gives a reason for cautious interpretation.
worked_examples.meaning: The wording preserves useful information while acknowledging uncertainty.

common_mistakes.draft: Both sources mention the room, so they prove the same thing.
common_mistakes.revision: Identify what each source actually measured.
common_mistakes.reason: A shared topic does not imply identical evidence.

common_mistakes.draft: A source is credible because its title sounds academic.
common_mistakes.revision: Check the source, method and relevance to the specific claim.
common_mistakes.reason: Presentation alone does not establish reliability.

takeaways: Match evidence to the exact claim.

lessons.title: Revise meaning before polishing words
lessons.purpose: Improve a paragraph in a sequence that protects meaning, organisation and accuracy.
explanation: Revision and proofreading address different levels. Revision asks whether the text answers its purpose, develops the right ideas and uses valid evidence. Proofreading checks sentence-level details such as agreement, punctuation and spelling. Correcting spelling first can leave a polished paragraph that still makes an unsupported claim.

Review in a useful order: purpose and coverage; logic and paragraph order; facts and numerical values; sentence meaning; grammar and punctuation. Read the final version again to ensure that a local edit has not changed a number or removed an important condition. A checklist helps attention, but it does not certify that the writing is error-free.

Editing should preserve the author’s intended meaning when that meaning is supportable. When a claim is unsupported, revise the claim or find suitable evidence rather than merely replacing a strong verb with another impressive verb. Clear writing often results from deleting a repetition and naming an ambiguous reference.

language_pattern.form: Purpose → structure → evidence → sentence clarity → final proofreading.
language_pattern.meaning: Fix the largest problem before the smallest one.
language_pattern.limits: The sequence is a practical aid, not an automated quality or grade assessment.

worked_examples.title: An annotated complete revision
worked_examples.context: Invented draft: “The survey prove the room is perfect. 12 students like it. This means grades increased. It is very useful and useful.” Context: 18 volunteers answered a preference survey; 12 preferred the room; grades were not measured.
worked_examples.model: In a preference survey of 18 volunteers, 12 preferred the room. This result suggests that the space was useful to some respondents, but the survey did not measure grades. Further feedback would help explain which features they valued.
annotations: The opening restores the missing denominator and volunteer context.
Preferred reports the measured preference accurately.
The unsupported claim about grades is removed.
The repetition is replaced with a relevant next information need.
worked_examples.meaning: The revised paragraph is stronger because its claim is more defensible, not because its words are longer.

worked_examples.title: Repair a dangling opening phrase
worked_examples.context: Draft: “After checking the graph, the error became clear.” The intended checker was the student.
worked_examples.model: After checking the graph, the student identified the error.
annotations: The opening action now belongs to the subject that follows.
The student supplies the missing actor.
The revision describes what became clear through an explicit action.
worked_examples.meaning: An introductory phrase should attach to the intended subject.

common_mistakes.draft: The spelling is correct, so the argument must be correct.
common_mistakes.revision: Check the reasoning and evidence separately from spelling.
common_mistakes.reason: Different kinds of quality require different checks.

common_mistakes.draft: Replace every repeated technical term with a synonym.
common_mistakes.revision: Repeat a precise technical term when a synonym could change its meaning.
common_mistakes.reason: Consistency can help the reader follow an argument.

takeaways: Revise the claim before polishing its surface.
Preserve clear reference and consistent terminology.
